[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Architecting Background Jobs in Ruby on Rails: Active Job vs. Sidekiq"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When building scalable Ruby on Rails applications, offloading time-consuming tasks like sending emails, processing payments, or generating reports to background workers is essential. Rails provides Active Job as a unified abstraction layer, while Sidekiq is a high-performance background processing framework powered by Redis. Understanding how they work together is critical for building resilient systems."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Active Job"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Active Job is a framework for declaring jobs and making them run on a variety of queuing backends. It acts as an adapter layer. By writing your jobs using Active Job, you can switch your underlying queuing system (from Delayed Job to Sidekiq, for example) without changing your job implementation logic."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Provides a standard interface for job creation and execution."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Supports global ID serialization for Active Record objects."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Includes built-in hooks for callbacks like before_enqueue and around_perform."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Sidekiq"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sidekiq is a full-featured background processing framework for Ruby. Unlike many traditional queue systems that rely on separate database tables, Sidekiq uses Redis as an in-memory data store. This design makes Sidekiq exceptionally fast and memory-efficient, capable of processing millions of jobs with minimal overhead through multithreading."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Setting Up Sidekiq as the Active Job Backend"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"To configure Sidekiq as your default Active Job backend, add the gem to your Gemfile and configure your application settings."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"# Gemfile
gem 'sidekiq'"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Next, update your configuration file to instruct Active Job to use Sidekiq."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# config/application.rb
module MyApp
  class Application < Rails::Application
    config.active_job.queue_adapter = :sidekiq
  end
end"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Generating and Writing a Job"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Use the Rails generator to create a new background job. This will create a file in app/jobs inheriting from ActiveJob::Base."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"bin/rails generate job ProcessPayment"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Implement the perform method inside your generated job file."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"# app/jobs/process_payment_job.rb
class ProcessPaymentJob < ApplicationJob
  queue_as :default

  def perform(user_id, amount)
    user = User.find(user_id)
    PaymentGateway.charge(user: user, amount: amount)
  end
end"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Enqueuing Jobs"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can enqueue your job to run asynchronously using the perform_later method. Active Job will serialize the arguments and push them to Redis via Sidekiq."},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"# Enqueue a job to be performed asynchronously
ProcessPaymentJob.perform_later(current_user.id, 9999)

# Enqueue a job to be performed after a delay
ProcessPaymentJob.set(wait: 5.minutes).perform_later(current_user.id, 9999)"},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Architecture"},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pass IDs instead of full model instances when dealing with volatile data to prevent stale state issues."},{"order":25,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keep jobs idempotent so that retrying a failed job does not cause unintended duplicate side effects."},{"order":26,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor your Sidekiq queues using the built-in Sidekiq Web UI protected by administrative authentication."}]
